entry: Country in [[West Africa]] (pop., 2024: 2,422,712), the smallest country in continental Africa. It is surrounded by [[Senegal]] except on the west, where it meets the [[Atlantic Ocean]]; its territory lies along both banks of the lower Gambia River. Banjul, formerly Bathurst, is the capital. The [[British Empire]] established a colony in 1765, and the Gambia became independent in 1965 under Dawda Jawara. Yahya Jammeh seized power in a bloodless coup on July 22, 1994. Adama Barrow defeated Jammeh in the December 2016 election, but Jammeh initially accepted the results and then refused to leave office. An intervention by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) achieved Jammeh's removal two days after his term was scheduled to end. The economy depends on farming, fishing and tourism. English is the sole official language. The country rejoined the [[Commonwealth of Nations|Commonwealth]] in 2018 after withdrawing in 2013.

Five-panel triptych by [[Hieronymus Bosch]], painted between 1490 and 1510. Closed, its outer panels show the Third Day of Creation in green-gray grisaille. Open, its inner panels show a paradise, a central panel of lustful humanity, and [[Hell]]. Interpretations usually treat the work as a warning against temptation, reflecting Bosch's religious beliefs, but twentieth-century art historians disagree over whether the central panel is a moral warning or a panorama of paradise lost. It is not known whether the painting was intended as an altarpiece, although its extreme subject matter makes a church or monastery an unlikely setting. The triptych has been housed in the [[Museo del Prado]] in Madrid since 1939.

headword: The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
sort_key: general theory of employment interest and money
entry: Book by English economist [[John Maynard Keynes]], published in February 1936. It argued that an economy does not automatically reach full employment, even in equilibrium, and that employment depends on the level of aggregate demand rather than on the price of labor. The book is a sustained attack on the classical economics of its time. It introduced the consumption function, the principle of effective demand, liquidity preference and the multiplier. Its concepts gave [[Macroeconomics|macroeconomics]] a central place in economic theory and contributed much of its terminology. The book was interpreted as supporting government spending, budget deficits and countercyclical policy, and its influence is known as the "Keynesian Revolution." The work is pervaded by mistrust of the rationality of free-market decision-making.

Brazilian [[Bossa nova|bossa nova]] song with music by [[Antônio Carlos Jobim]] and Portuguese lyrics by Vinícius de Moraes, written in 1962. Its original title was "Menina que Passa," and it was inspired by a 17-year-old woman who walked past a café in Ipanema on her way to the beach. A recording by Stan Getz, with the vocal debut of Astrud Gilberto singing English lyrics by Norman Gimbel, became an international hit. Gilberto was never credited and was paid only $120 for her part. The single peaked at number five on the Billboard Hot 100, and the song won a Grammy for Record of the Year in 1965. It is believed to be the second-most-recorded pop song in history, after "Yesterday" by [[The Beatles]]. In 2004 the [[Library of Congress]] added the recording to its National Recording Registry.

1972 American crime film directed by [[Francis Ford Coppola]], adapted with Mario Puzo from Puzo's 1969 novel. It follows the Corleone family, a Mafia family, as the youngest son, Michael ([[Al Pacino]]), turns from a reluctant outsider into its ruthless head. [[Marlon Brando]] plays Vito Corleone. Much of the film was shot in New York City and [[Sicily]]. It premiered on March 14, 1972, and was the highest-grossing film of 1972; for a time it was the highest-grossing film ever made, earning between $250 and $291 million. It won the Academy Award for Best Picture, and Brando won Best Actor. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 1990, and the American Film Institute ranked it second only to [[Citizen Kane]] among American films. It was followed by *The Godfather Part II* (1974).

1974 American crime film directed by [[Francis Ford Coppola]], both a sequel and a prequel to *The Godfather* (1972). Its parallel stories follow Michael Corleone ([[Al Pacino]]) in 1958, and the youth of his father, Vito, played by [[Robert De Niro]], from Sicily to [[New York City]]. The film received 11 Academy Award nominations and won six, including Best Picture, making it the first sequel to win that award. It grossed $48 million in the United States and Canada on a budget of $13 million. The American Film Institute ranked it the 32nd-greatest film in American history.

[[Latin]] novel by Apuleius, the only ancient Roman novel in Latin to survive in its entirety. Also titled *Metamorphoses*, it was called *The Golden Ass* by [[Augustine of Hippo]]. Its narrator, Lucius, is driven by curiosity and a desire to practice [[Magic (supernatural)|magic]]. While trying to perform a spell to become a bird, he is accidentally transformed into a [[Donkey|donkey]]. His long journey includes inset tales, and he finds salvation through the goddess [[Isis]], whose cult he joins. The text survives in about 40 manuscripts, nearly all descended from an 11th-century codex produced at Monte Cassino. Scholars date its composition variously, as an early work before Apuleius's *Apology* of 158–159 or as a late work of the 170s or 180s.

American [[Sitcom|sitcom]] (1985–1992) about four older women sharing a house in [[Miami]]. Created by Susan Harris for [[NBC]], it ran for seven seasons and 180 half-hour episodes. The ensemble cast included Bea Arthur, [[Betty White]], Rue McClanahan and Estelle Getty. The show won two Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Comedy Series and three Golden Globe Awards for Best Television Series – Musical or Comedy. All four lead actresses won Primetime Emmys, making it one of only four sitcoms in which all principal cast members received Emmy recognition. In 2013 TV Guide ranked it 54th among the 60 best series of all time.

headword: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
sort_key: good the bad and the ugly
entry: 1966 Italian epic [[Western (genre)|spaghetti Western]] film directed by Sergio Leone. [[Clint Eastwood]], Lee Van Cleef and Eli Wallach play three gunslingers who form shifting alliances in a search for a buried cache of Confederate gold during the [[American Civil War]]. It is the third and final installment of Leone's Dollars Trilogy, following *A Fistful of Dollars* (1964) and *For a Few Dollars More* (1965), although the films are connected thematically rather than by a continuous narrative. Filmed mainly in Spain, including at the purpose-built Sad Hill Cemetery set, it features a score by Ennio Morricone. It grossed over $38 million worldwide on a budget of about $1.2 million. Critics in some markets were initially mixed, but the film developed a strong cult following and is frequently cited as one of the greatest Western films of all time.

1967 American romantic comedy-drama directed by [[Mike Nichols]], adapted from Charles Webb's 1963 novella. It stars [[Dustin Hoffman]] as Benjamin Braddock, a recent college graduate who has an affair with the older Mrs. Robinson, played by [[Anne Bancroft]], before falling for her daughter, Elaine. The [[Simon & Garfunkel]] soundtrack includes the hit "Mrs. Robinson." It was the highest-grossing film of 1967 in North America, earning $104.9 million in the United States and Canada. It received seven nominations at the 40th [[Academy Awards]], and Nichols won Best Director. The [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry in 1996.

American realist novel by [[John Steinbeck]], published in 1939. Set during the [[Great Depression]], it follows the Joads, a family of tenant farmers driven from their [[Oklahoma]] home by drought, bank foreclosures and changes in agriculture. Trapped in the [[Dust Bowl]], they travel west on the "mother road" to [[California]] with thousands of other migrants, where they find an oversupply of labor, low wages and exploitation. The novel won the National Book Award and the Pulitzer Prize for fiction, and it was cited when Steinbeck received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1962. It is often listed among the greatest novels in English and is frequently read in American schools. A 1940 film starring [[Henry Fonda]] and directed by [[John Ford]] adapted it.

Novel by American writer [[F. Scott Fitzgerald]], published in 1925. Set in the Jazz Age on [[Long Island]], it follows narrator Nick Carraway's association with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby, who is obsessed with reuniting with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. Fitzgerald drew on a youthful romance and on the parties he attended on Long Island's North Shore in 1922. His editor, Maxwell Perkins, persuaded him to revise a 1924 draft. The novel was a commercial disappointment, selling fewer than 20,000 copies by October 1925. During [[World War II]] the Council on Books in Wartime distributed free copies to American soldiers overseas, and the book soon became a core part of most American high school curricula. Scholars emphasize its treatment of [[Social class|social class]], inherited versus self-made wealth, and its cynical attitude toward the American Dream.

Woodblock print by [[Hokusai]], created in late 1831 during the [[Edo period]]. It is the first print in his series *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*. It depicts three boats in a storm-tossed sea, with a large cresting wave forming a spiral above them and [[Mount Fuji]] in the background. The use of [[Prussian blue]] revolutionized Japanese prints, and the composition synthesizes traditional Japanese prints with graphical perspective developed in Europe. It influenced Western artists and musicians, including [[Claude Monet]], [[Claude Debussy]] and [[Vincent van Gogh]]. Only about 100 prints, in varying condition, are thought to survive. The work has been described as "possibly the most reproduced image in the history of all art."

British national daily newspaper, founded in [[Manchester]] in 1821 as *The Manchester Guardian*. The Scott Trust, created in 1936 to protect its editorial independence, owns it, and profits are reinvested in journalism. It is considered a newspaper of record in the UK and has been named newspaper of the year four times at the British Press Awards. Its reporting broke the 2011 News International phone-hacking scandal, and in 2013 it revealed the PRISM surveillance program after information from [[Edward Snowden]]. In 2016 it led the Panama Papers investigation, which exposed then-prime minister [[David Cameron]]'s links to offshore bank accounts.

Capital city of South Holland province, in the western [[Netherlands]]. It is the third-largest city in the country, with over half a million residents. [[Amsterdam]] is the official capital, but The Hague has been the de facto seat of government since the Dutch Republic, and it houses the Cabinet, the States General, the Supreme Court and the Council of State. Most foreign embassies in the Netherlands are in the city. Located on the [[North Sea]] coast, it includes the seaside resort of Scheveningen. The city is a center of international law: the [[International Court of Justice]] and the [[International Criminal Court]] are based there, along with about 200 other international organizations. It hosted the 2014 Nuclear Security Summit and the 2025 NATO Summit.

Dystopian novel by Canadian author [[Margaret Atwood]], published in 1985. It is set in the Republic of Gilead, a patriarchal, totalitarian state that overthrew the United States government in a near-future [[New England]]. Its protagonist, Offred, is a Handmaid, a woman forcibly assigned to bear children for a Commander. Its title echoes the component parts of [[Geoffrey Chaucer]]'s *The Canterbury Tales*. It won the 1985 Governor General's Award and the first Arthur C. Clarke Award in 1987. A 2017 television series adapted the story, and the sequel *The Testaments* was published in 2019.

headword: The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire
sort_key: history of the decline and fall of the roman empire
entry: Six-volume work of history by English historian [[Edward Gibbon]]. It covers the period from 98 to 1590, from the peak of the [[Roman Empire]] through the rise of Christianity as the state religion, the fall of the Western Roman Empire, and the rise of [[Genghis Khan]] and the fall of Byzantium. Gibbon argued that the empire succumbed to barbarian invasions largely because its citizens gradually lost civic virtue, and he gave great weight to other internal causes of decline and to outside attacks. His treatment of Christianity began a continuing controversy. Volume I was published in February 1776, and the final three volumes appeared together in 1788. Gibbon's tone is detached and dispassionate yet critical, and he occasionally lapses into moralization and aphorism.

headword: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy
entry: Comedy science fiction franchise created by Douglas Adams. It began as a [[BBC]] Radio 4 sitcom in 1978 and was adapted into novels, a 1981 BBC television series, a 1984 text adventure game and a 2005 feature film. The novels have been translated into more than 30 languages. The plot follows Arthur Dent, the last surviving [[Earth]] man, who is rescued by his alien friend Ford Prefect before the planet is demolished for a hyperspace bypass. Together they travel the galaxy with Trillian and Zaphod Beeblebrox. Audiobooks are narrated by [[Stephen Fry]].

Children's fantasy novel by English author [[J. R. R. Tolkien]], published in 1937. The home-loving hobbit Bilbo Baggins joins the wizard [[Gandalf]] and thirteen dwarves led by Thorin Oakenshield on a quest to reclaim their treasure from the dragon Smaug. The episodic story climaxes in the Battle of Five Armies. Nominated for the Carnegie Medal, the book is recognized as a classic of children's literature and has sold over 100 million copies. Revisions for the second edition aligned it more closely with *The Lord of the Rings*, on which Tolkien was working.

Genocide of European Jews by [[Nazi Germany]] and its collaborators during [[World War II]]. From 1941 to 1945 the Nazis systematically murdered about six million Jews, roughly two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population. The murders were committed primarily through mass shootings in Eastern Europe and poison gas chambers at extermination camps in occupied Poland. After the Wannsee Conference, presided over by [[Reinhard Heydrich]], the [[Final Solution]] to murder all Jews in Europe was implemented by early 1942. The Nazis also persecuted and murdered millions of others, including Roma and Soviet prisoners of war. Relatively few perpetrators faced criminal trials, and billions of dollars in reparations have been paid. The Holocaust is considered the deadliest genocide in human history.

headword: The House of the Rising Sun
entry: American traditional folk song, also called "Rising Sun Blues." It tells of a life gone wrong in [[New Orleans]], and many versions urge a sibling or children to avoid the same fate. It was first collected in [[Appalachia]] in the 1930s and probably has roots in English folk song. The 1964 version by the English rock band The Animals reached number one in the UK, the US and Canada, and it has been described as the "first folk rock hit." Earlier versions were recorded by [[Woody Guthrie]], [[Joan Baez]], [[Bob Dylan]] and [[Nina Simone]].

Gothic novel by [[Victor Hugo]], published in 1831 as *Notre-Dame de Paris*. Set in [[Paris]] in 1482 during the reign of [[Louis XI]], it follows the bell-ringer Quasimodo, the Romani street dancer Esmeralda and the archdeacon Claude Frollo, whose obsessive lust for Esmeralda drives him toward ruin. Hugo wrote it to champion the preservation of [[Gothic architecture]], and the novel helped make the cathedral a national icon. It is considered a classic of French literature and has been adapted repeatedly for film, stage and television, including a 1939 sound film with [[Charles Laughton]] and a 1956 film with [[Anthony Quinn]].

Young adult dystopian novel series by American author Suzanne Collins. Set in Panem, a post-apocalyptic North American nation divided between a wealthy Capitol and 12 districts, the trilogy follows teenager Katniss Everdeen. Each district must send two children to the Capitol's annual battle royale, and the last survivor is dubbed the victor. The trilogy comprises *The Hunger Games* (2008), *Catching Fire* (2009) and *Mockingjay* (2010). Each book was adapted into a film, starring [[Jennifer Lawrence]] as Katniss. The series had sold over 100 million copies worldwide by 2023. Two prequels have been published, the most recent in 2025.

Landmark 11th-century critique of Islamic philosophy by [[Al-Ghazali]], written c. 1095. Al-Ghazali, a theologian of the Asharite school, criticizes the Avicennian school, denouncing [[Avicenna]] and [[Al-Farabi]] for following Greek philosophy when it appears to contradict Islam. The book is organized into 20 discussions. It accuses the philosophers of heresy on 17 points and of irreligion in three others. It favors faith over philosophy in matters of [[Metaphysics]] and knowledge of the divine. The work marked a milestone in the rise of the Asharite school, and it was answered by [[Averroes]] in *The Incoherence of the Incoherence*.

American family pop group formed in Gary, Indiana, in 1964 as the Jackson Brothers. Its members were Jackie, Tito, Jermaine, Marlon and [[Michael Jackson]], managed by their father, Joe Jackson. After signing with [[Motown]] in 1968, they became the first group to debut with four consecutive number-one hits on the Billboard Hot 100: "I Want You Back," "ABC," "The Love You Save" and "I'll Be There." The group left Motown for Epic Records in 1976 and became the Jacksons. It has sold over 150 million records worldwide and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 1997.
